However, accurately determining the visibility of quantum foam effects, a phenomenon related to the theoretical model known as quantum gravity, within these simulations is challenging. A group of researchers recently used an analytical approach to examine the relationship between scalar gravitational waves and scalar matter fields in a dynamic, merged black hole scenario. They then applied this approach to a simplified model of two merging black holes and investigated the possibility of detecting quantum foam effects through gravitational waves. Although the effects were found to be very faint and likely undetectable with the most sensitive future gravitational wave detectors. Nonetheless, this study provides a framework for assessing the visibility of quantum foam effects within black hole merger events.  To further analyze the phenomenon, the researchers also explored different spin velocities of the black holes and various masses of the matter fields, discovering that the visibility of quantum foam effects is more likely during the point when the two black holes merge into one. Furthermore, this study highlights the necessity for improved sensitivity in future gravitational wave detectors if they are to detect quantum foam effects, a mark that LISA is expected to achieve in the future.   for emerging situations involving uncharted datasets. This problem is similar to 
  that faced in natural language processing's vocabulary acquisition issue. One 
  potential solution to this problem is training a universal detector on a broadly 
  defined set of classes, which can facilitate the detection of novel objects. 
  This approach relies on few-shot learning methods to achieve this goal. In this 
  research, we investigate the possibility of training a universal detector on a 
  small set of classes with the ability to adapt to novel objects from a large, 
  unstructured dataset. We achieve this by integrating a multi-scale attention 
  mechanism into the feature fusion block of the one-to-many object detection 
  network, which enables the detector to focus on novel regions of the image. 
  We dub this integrated system TAO. We further develop a novel method, known as 
  supervised few-shot adaptation, to fine-tune the universal detector on a small 
  set of labeled data. We evaluate TAO on the novel object detection dataset 
  COX19 and the few-shot object detection dataset VISOFF. The results show that 
  TAO compares favorably to the one-to-many object detection network in detection 
  accuracy as measured by the AP score, with a 13.7% improvement on the COX19 
  dataset.  We also find that TAO generalizes well to the few-shot setting, with 
  a 10.5% increase in AP score on the VISOFF dataset at the 20-way, 500-shot 
  protocol.  We believe that our research on a universal detector can serve as

  Although the term "Learning the Law" could refer to various interpretations, 
  in this context, it means discovering the underlying dynamics and statistics 
  that govern a stochastic process, often based on partial and noisy observations. 
  This learning process can result in the derivation of explicit, data-driven 
  equations that represent the underlying dynamics and statistics, which in turn 
  enable the prediction of future observations and the estimation of hidden 
  variables. This approach to law learning contrasts with methods that utilize 
  supervised learning, even when the underlying dynamics are deterministic. 

  Throughout this introduction, we will use "statistics" to refer to the 
  probabilistic properties that govern a stochastic process, such as the 
  distribution over possible states and the rules that govern transitions between 
  those states. 

  ## Scalar vs. Vector PLD

  Two primary variations of PLD exist: scalar and vector. Scalar PLD involves 
  the learning of a single equation that represents the underlying dynamics of a 
  stochastic process, often in the form of a difference equation. This learning 
  process can result in the derivation of an explicit, data-driven version of 
  this equation, which in turn enables the prediction of future observations and 
  the estimation of hidden variables. 

  In contrast, vector PLD is concerned with the learning of multiple equations 
  that represent the underlying dynamics of a stochastic process. This learning 
  process can result in the derivation of explicit, data-driven versions of these 
  equations, which in turn enable the prediction of future observations, the 
  estimation of hidden variables, and the characterization of the statistics 
  governing the process.

  This research focuses on analyzing the structural elements of well-defined jokes
  using a linguistic approach, with a key aspect being the identification of
  linguistic markers that distinguish setup from punchline. A significant finding
  is that a well-defined joke's setup and punchline are often connected by a
  specific type of clause that cannot stand alone, suggesting that the core
  relationship between setup and punchline is governed by a particular type of
  relational clause. A statistical examination using a machine learning model
  reveals that this characteristic holds value in predicting whether a joke is
  well-defined. Interestingly, this feature does not significantly impact the
  task of classifying jokes as either well-defined or multi-part. Furthermore,
  exploring the context of dialogue systems that generate jokes, we found that
  incorporating this feature leads to improvements in the overall coherence
  (CoH) score in evaluations. A subsequent manual analysis of generated joke
  coherence reveals that this feature's integration results in more coherent jokes
  in the middle part of the conversation. It is worth noting that this finding
  does not necessarily imply a systematic pattern. Consequently, future research
  is needed to establish a relationship between dialogue progression and joke
  coherence. Additionally, manual analysis of generated jokes' coherence highlights
  the challenge of distinguishing between jokes that are inherently coherent and
  those that are so due to other factors such as context familiarity.  Finally,
  a proposed model that incorporates this feature is presented, along with
  manual analysis results discussing its strengths and limitations. A possible
  extension to the model is also explored and shown to improve coherence in
  generated jokes. However, this improvement is not consistently observed in
  manual evaluations. Consequently, future research is needed to further refine
  dialogue systems that generate jokes in a coherent manner. A theoretical

  and gated recurrent units for modeling long-range dependencies in sequence learning tasks.
  However, the fundamental limitation of RNN architectures, specifically the sequential
  nature of weight matrix multiplication, restricts their application in situations requiring
  the analysis of vast amounts of data. To address this constraint, we present a novel
  RNN architecture, referred to as Vector-Vector LSTM (VV-LSTM), that enables parallelized
  learning across vast datasets. The proposed VV-LSTM design leverages the capabilities
  of multi-head attention to facilitate the fusion of processed vector representations, 
  thereby allowing for the use of weight matrix multiplication in a parallelized manner. 
  We have thoroughly evaluated the vector-vector LSTM model through a range of tasks, 
  including dense representation learning in vast datasets, along with stepped knowledge 
  graph constructions, and our findings demonstrate a notable improvement in performance 
  compared to traditional RNN architectures.  We have made the code publicly available at 
  https://github.com/ghrua/VectorVectorLSTM.

  investigations reveal that the underlying mechanism is difficult to analyze, thereby

  alleviate this challenge, we have developed a simplified vector-valued RNN architecture 
  referred to as Vector-Vector F-LSTM (VV-F-LSTM), which we have found to be more 
  tractable in our experiments. The proposed VV-F-LSTM design can be utilized for 
  dense representation learning, and we have made the code publicly available at 
  https://github.com/ghrua/VectorVectorFLSTM.

  that rapid rotation in young M-dwarf stars leads to binary systems and 
  stabilizes the orbits of objects in the star's gravitational influence, 
  incorporating super-Earths and Neptune-sized planets. Ultimately, the findings

  This paper proves that in any connected, bipartite graph without triangles,
  there exists a perfect matching cut, assuming the graph's every vertex has
  a high enough degree. This result extends a previous finding by Kühn, Tregear,
  and Wloch, which demonstrated the existence of a perfect matching cut in
  large, loop-free bipartite graphs without triangles, provided the graph's
  every edge was connected to a large enough vertex set. To achieve this
  extension, the proof relies on a more refined version of the general
  theorem by Galasso, which in turn is based on a result from the work
  by Kühn, Tregear, and Wloch. Additionally, this paper presents sharp
  degree requirements and provides an infinite series of examples to
  illustrate the tightness of these requirements. Furthermore, it also
  shows that in a larger, bipartite graph without triangles, if the
  graph's every vertex has a degree within a certain high range, it
  will contain multiple perfect matching cuts, as well as a set of
  disjoint loops, and it presents a way to extend this result to
  graphs with triangles. A research note on this topic has been
  posted on the arXiv preprint server. A connected, bipartite graph
  without triangles is a type of 2-degenerate graph. A result from
  the work by Galasso implies that a connected, 2-degenerate graph
  with a high enough maximum degree will contain a subgraph that is
  a collection of loops without any outside edges. This fact, along
  with the properties of a 2-degenerate graph, allows one to find
  a subcollection of loops that are internally connected and have
  a high enough size to be considered a forest. However, as it
  turns out, being a forest is not sufficient for a graph to
  have a perfect matching cut, which is why an additional
  condition is needed, and it is provided by the requirement
  that the graph's every edge is connected to a large enough
  vertex set. This condition is crucial, as it ensures
  that any loop in the graph will share an edge with
  another loop, which in turn guarantees the existence
  of a perfect matching cut.

This model accounts for exotic hadron reservations through specific cross-sections and decay patterns. In our analysis, we consider three types of expansions: isolated expansions in $L$ and $T$ directions, and combined expansions in both directions. Our study focuses on exotic hadron reservations at two different temperatures ($T=140$ MeV and $T=180$ MeV). At $T=140$ MeV, we observe that the ratio of charged particle density to entropy density is higher in the combined expansion scenario than in the isolated expansion scenario. However, this difference decreases as the temperature increases. Furthermore, our results show that the effect of longitudinal expansion is more significant than the effect of transverse expansion on the ratio of charged particle density to entropy density. This phenomenon is more pronounced at lower temperatures. However, the difference between the results of the combined expansion and the isolated expansion scenarios diminishes as the temperature increases. This phenomenon can be attributed to the increase in pion production at higher temperatures, which contributes more significantly to the expansion. Our study also compares our results with existing data and models, such as hadron resonance cascade (HRC) model, thermal QCD model, and exponential fit to thermal data. In summary, our study emphasizes the importance of incorporating exotic hadron reservations into thermal models, especially at higher densities, and suggests that such reservations could be a crucial factor in understanding the properties of highly excited matter. Moreover, our findings imply that exotic hadron reservations could influence the behavior of expanding systems in high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions. Consequently, future thermal models should take into account exotic hadron reservations across a broader range of temperatures and densities to ensure a more accurate representation of experimental data. This is particularly crucial for evaluating exotic hadron reservations in scenarios with multiple interactions, such as those present in central lead-lead collisions. In such cases, models should be capable of simulating correctly not only thermal scenarios but also scenarios with higher densities and energies per particle. Furthermore, our study suggests that future thermal models should account for exemptions from normal hadronization in systems with exotic hadron reservations. In contrast, models that employ cross-sections based solely on temperature per particle may overestimate exotic hadron reservations in systems with higher energies per particle. In conclusion, our study emphasizes the necessity of integrating exotic hadron reservations into thermal models to ensure a more accurate interpretation of data from high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions.   them.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in a wide

three specific problems:
  The first, known as the Generalized Minimum Circulant Problem, involves finding the smallest circulant matrix that contains a given vector, a so-called "ghost vector". The second, the hidden periodic structure problem, involves identifying periodic structures within a vector, given a set of linear operators. The third, the circulant embedding problem, involves placing a vector within the smallest circulant matrix while factoring a set of linear operators. The thesis develops a quantum algorithm for solving each of these problems. The comparisons with classical counterparts reveal exponential speedup in solving the first and second problems using a quantum computer. The thesis also explores the #P-hardness of the circulant embedding problem. The thesis further delves into the implementation of these algorithms using a specific set of linear operators known as the Fourier Smoothing operator. The appendix of the thesis provides the detailed implementation along with additional mathematical proofs.   Understanding protein architecture is crucial for addressing various medical

  artificial intelligence have made it possible to quickly build and test various
  protein structures using artificial templates. However, existing methods often
  produce molecules that are biologically impossible. To address this challenge,
  a new machine learning technique called ProtTASS was developed. ProtTASS
  generates protein structures that are not only visually similar to a given
  reference structure, but also comply with chemical rules and biological
  functionality. In experiments, ProtTASS demonstrated an impressive capacity
  to replicate the architecture of proteins already known to science, as well as
  design novel protein structures that successfully perform specific tasks.  |

  This research paper introduces ProtTASS, a novel artificial intelligence tool
  capable of constructing protein structures based on examples, with results shown
  below.

  **Code and Data**

  To reproduce the outcomes presented in this study, the code for ProtTASS is
  available at https://github.com/wangxu2018/ProtTASS, along with the
  trained models and test data.

  **Example Usage**

  To generate a protein structure similar to a given template, you can use the
  command line interface of ProtTASS as follows:

  ```
  python generate.py --template PDBFOLD_ID --similar PDB_ID --output output_PDB_ID
  ```

  For instance, to create a protein structure similar to the one with PDB ID
  6W9Y, you can run the command:

  ```
  python generate.py --template 6W9Y --similar 6W9Y --output test_PDB_ID
  ```

  **Training ProtTASS**

  To train a custom ProtTASS model for a specific protein target, you need to
  prepare a dataset with correctly aligned protein structures and prepare the
  corresponding input files in the required format, then run the training
  script as follows:

  ```
  python train.py --data data_dir --model model_file --descriptors descriptors_file
  ```

  For instance, to train a model for the protein target with PDB ID 6W9Y, you
  can run the command:

  ```
  python train.py --data data_dir --model model_file --descriptors descriptors_file
  ```

performed with a non-toxic computational fluid dynamics tool to model the behavior of water contaminated with algae toxins in a specific scenario. The scenario involves a stagnant layer of water on a lake bed, subjected to heat from the surface through a defined layer, also known as the "epilimnion." The goal of the analysis is to determine the rate at which toxins release heat and spread to the deeper waters of the lake. The analysis accounts for two types of water movement: gentle currents that circulate water within the lake and a layer of water that remains stagnant on the bed. The analysis was conducted over an eight-day period and showed that the rate at which heat is released by the toxins affects the movement of the stagnant water layer, causing it to move downwards more quickly. However, even with this downward movement, the deeper waters of the lake remain vulnerable to pollution. The analysis suggests that a combination of climate change, water circulation, and the behavior of water plants could exacerbate the problem of pollution in lakes. The code used for the analysis is included as an appendix. The analysis was conducted with a code based on a finite element method and a Navier-Stokes equation to model the movements of the water, a heat equation to model the temperature of the water, and an advection-diffusion equation to model the dispersion of the toxin. The code was run on a three-dimensional grid of water but the results shown here are two-dimensional. The analysis was performed with a code that can handle complex geometric shapes and a large disparity in water currents. The code used for the analysis is a version of the free and open-source software Fenics. The analysis was validated with previous studies and an experimental study published in 1996. To efficiently capture these seasonal patterns, we introduce a novel neural network component called the Periodic Coattention Module (PCAM).   environment.

  $B = \{a^2 \mid a \in A\}$, what is the name of the collection of
  subsets of $B$ that are countable, given that $A$ is uncountable?  This
  collection of subsets of $B$ is sometimes referred to as $\mathcal{P}_\kappa
  (B)$, where $\kappa$ denotes the cardinality of $A$.  In this case, we
  have $\mathcal{P}_\kappa (B) \simeq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, where
  $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is the power set of the set of natural numbers.  A
  notable result from set theory is that the power set of an uncountable set is
  also uncountable, a fact that can be derived from Cantor's theorem, which
  states that for any set $X$, the function $f: X \to \mathcal{P}(X)$ defined
  by $f(x) = \{x\}$ is not injective.  In other words, the cardinality of
  $\mathcal{P}(X)$ is strictly greater than the cardinality of $X$ for any
  set $X$ that is not the empty set.  With this in mind, we can see that
  $\mathcal{P}_\kappa (B) \simeq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is not simply the
  collection of countable subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, as this would have the
  same cardinality as $\mathbb{N}$ itself.  Rather, it represents the
  collection of subsets of $B$ that are countable, given that $A$ is
  uncountable, and we can think of this as the power set of the set of
  natural numbers, which, as noted earlier, is uncountable.  In this case,
  we can also see that the power set of the set of natural numbers, which is
  the collection of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, has the same cardinality as the
  collection of subsets of $B$ that are countable, given that $A$ is
  uncountable.

In this research, we investigate the non-convexity of FWI by analyzing the distances between synthetic data and the actual data recorded during seismic surveys, formulated within a convex optimization framework. This indicates that the non-convexity of FWI is linked to the $l_2$-distance measure used rather than the wave equation's nonlinearity.  As such, we suggest modifying the distance measure in the convex optimization framework to make it more aligned with the physics of seismic data generation, which could potentially alleviate the local minimum traps encountered in FWI.  Furthermore, this modification can be viewed as a regularizer that penalizes deviations from the expected reflectivity series, thereby stabilizing the FWI algorithm.  Our results are validated using synthetic data and the Marmousi23 model. As such, the proposed modification to the distance measure presents an promising strategy for developing robust and physically consistent FWI algorithms. Current state-of-the-art models are restricted by their inability to process video inputs efficiently, lacking an effective multi-stream fusion mechanism that integrates spatial and temporal information across different resolution levels. To address this limitation, we present a novel model called Efficient Multi-Scale Fusion Network (EMFN) that seamlessly fuses spatial and temporal information through a hierarchical, stream-to-stream architecture, allowing for the efficient deployment of large neural networks on a wide range of devices. Experimental evaluations on the Unity3D game platform and real-world video datasets showcase the superior performance and efficiency of the proposed EMFN model. Specifically, it exhibits a notable gain in achievement levels when trained on significantly reduced data sets, coupled with a record-breaking compression ratio achieved in the Unity3D benchmark. The proposed method also surpasses the current benchmark in EMNIST and CIFAR-10 image classification tasks, in addition to displaying remarkable generalization capabilities in real-world video classification tasks. anomalous deviation from standard model
  predictions in a rare decay, specifically the process $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$.
  To accomplish this, the LHCb experiment used a dataset of 1.0/fb of data collected
  at the LHC. Normally, this decay happens very quickly and is difficult to detect,
  but an anomaly in previous results sparked interest in this rare event.
  Following the initial findings, the current study raises the lower limit on the
  probability of this decay occurring from $4.3 \times 10^{-8}$ to $9.4 \times 10^{-8}$.
  Additionally, the research establishes an upper limit on the rare process $B^0_s \to e^+e^-$
  at $3.5 \times 10^{-7}$, and sets thresholds for discovering these events with
  even greater rarity in the future. 
  Since the $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay occurs at the same rate as $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$,
  a combined analysis of both experiments with increased data collection is expected
  to significantly lower the probability threshold. 
  The search for these rare events also helps understand the interconversion of
  $B^0_s$ and $B^0$ states, and the stability of these particles over time. 
  The LHCb findings are in line with standard model predictions and do not indicate
  any alternative physics theories. 
  To discover these events with even greater rarity, the LHCb experiment needs
  to collect more data at the current collision intensity levels. 
  Doing so will likely lower the probability threshold to $6.4 \times 10^{-8}$ 
  for the $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay. 
  The research also includes a search for the rare decay $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ 
  with an energy range that indicates a probability threshold of less than $20 \times 10^{-8}$, 
  and an analysis of the decay $B^0_s \to \phi\phi$ that establishes an upper limit 
  at $5.4 \times 10^{-5}$. 
  The LHCb experiment is well-positioned to significantly lower these thresholds 
  with the larger datasets it will collect in the future.

  However, applying these models to free-form text-based image manipulation guidance remains a significant challenge, particularly when extensive guidance is required.
  To tackle this issue, a novel approach called TURBO has been developed that employs a large language model in an iterative process to refine image manipulation.
  TURBO incorporates both the language model and a discriminator that assesses the relevance of the user's guidance to the resulting image, effectively preventing the model from learning to follow arbitrary text suggestions.
  As a result, the model excels at adhering to complex, multi-step guidance discussed in natural language dialogue, yielding high-quality outcomes even when faced with lengthy guidance.
  Notably, TURBO's performance surpasses that of a conditionally true language model that ensures the generated text is coherent and grammatically correct, yet falls short in ensuring the image accurately reflects the intended description.
  To evaluate TURBO's performance, a comprehensive dataset has been created that allows for the comparison of different models in their ability to learn from free-form text-based guidance discussed in natural language dialogue.
  As demonstrated in various experiments, TURBO's unique design leads to outstanding results in the face of guidance that is repetitive, conditionally dependent, and emotionally charged, as well as, importantly, free-form.  We believe that TURBO's success and the resulting dataset will greatly benefit researchers working on the intricate relationship between language and image manipulation.  As evidence, we show that TURBO's individual components can be valuable for a wide range of tasks, including, notably, large-scale conditional language generation where the condition varies significantly. Despite their widespread use, these apps suffer from several drawbacks in dealing with key transmission risks.  A fundamental problem they face is the exclusion of contacts acquired through inadequate symptom manifestation periods, crucial for identifying secondary transmissions during the initial stages of the pandemic.  To address this issue, we propose a statistical framework that estimates the distribution of symptom manifestation periods based on reported cases and fatalities data from the Covid-19 pandemic.  Specifically, we employ the Weibull distribution to model these periods and gauge the effectiveness of various distribution variants through goodness-of-fit tests and the $R$-squared metric.  The resulting parameterized function is integrated into a computational tool that can be utilized for predictive analysis of symptom manifestation periods across different geographical regions and time periods.  The corresponding code has been made publicly available on a repository platform.  The proposed approach can be used to guide the development of contact tracing apps and similar public health interventions that take into account the characteristics of symptom manifestation periods in pandemic transmission.  The methodology has been demonstrated through a geographical case study involving Australia. We examine the strategy of active voters who share information with each other but not with the decision-makers, in an attempt to influence their choice.  We investigate the equilibrium outcomes of this process and compare them to the results that would occur if the active voters had complete freedom to share information without restriction.  We show that in cases where the preferences of the voters are clear cut, the process converges to the same outcome as if they were sharing information without restriction.  However, among cases where the preferences are not clear cut, the process may converge to a different outcome, depending on the specific details of the situation.  We also analyze the strategy of the active voters in depth and derive conditions under which their preferred outcome can be achieved.  We illustrate the applicability of our findings to real world situations with multiple time periods and group dynamics.  We further analyze the process from the perspective of the passive voters and investigate the condition under which they benefit from the reduction in information sharing.  We show that this situation can arise even when the preferences of the voters are not completely clear cut.  We also explore the implications of our findings for the effect that the process has on the overall social welfare.  We investigate methods of improving the outcome of the process and analyze the role of partial information sharing as a mechanism of constraint that influences the behavior of the active voters.  We show that this mechanism enhances their truthfulness and provide conditions under which it leads to the outcome that maximizes the overall social welfare.  We illustrate this with an example.  We further analyze the process from a computational perspective and investigate the difficulty of determining the equilibrium outcome in full detail.  We show that this can be done efficiently when the preferences of the voters are clear cut, but that it can become challenging when the preferences are not completely clear cut.  We also explore approaches to approximating the equilibrium outcome and show that this can be done in a computationally efficient manner even when the preferences of the voters are not completely clear cut.  We investigate methods of implementing the process in full detail and show that this can be done through the use of payment schemes that are based on the mechanism of reinforcement learning.  We further analyze the financial implications of using these payment schemes and show that this can result in a situation where the process is used excessively even when it is not completely clear cut, to the detriment of the overall social welfare. Perot cavity was utilized in an investigation of quantum fluctuations in an interacting many-body system. By applying a combination of single-body driving forces, researchers stabilized a coherent state within the cavity, leading to a non-equilibrium steady state defined by a constant number of phonons in the cavity. In a recent study, authors analyzed the dynamics of this state in the presence of cavity phonons through a quantum lattice gas model. A distinctive phenomenon - the quenching of Tonalli noise - was observed in this system. Tonalli noise refers to the random diffusion of density ripples observed in classical simulations of the lattice gas model. This noise is produced by the fluctuations of the cavity field, and its absence is indicated by the formation of dense packets of energy that move through the system slowly. These results were demonstrated numerically using a discrete lattice approach and verified through an analytical study of a continuous model. In the absence of the driving force, these packets of energy become entangled with the cavity field, resulting in a state known as a photon bunch. This state can be stabilized and may be useful in experiments aimed at visualizing density ripples through an output port of the cavity. In such an experiment, the photon bunch would need to be generated continuously, and this may be challenging as it requires a precise balance between the driving force, the cavity non-linearity, and the photon number in the cavity. In conclusion, the quenching of Tonalli noise provides a clear indicator of the presence of a coherent state within a cavity through the emission of light from the output port, and this may be useful in searches for this state in future experiments. Furthermore, this noise also manifests as a disorder in the spatial arrangement of particles, and it may be crucial in understanding experiments aimed at visualizing density ripples in a lattice gas system driven by a coherent state. In such an experiment, the disorder may switch from a random distribution of density ripples (indicative of the absence of the photon bunch) to an ordered distribution (indicative of the presence of the photon bunch) by adjusting the parameters of the driving force carefully. In addition to its potential use in searching for a coherent state, the quenching of Tonalli noise may also arise in other systems, and it can result from the interaction between a driven non-equilibrium system and a source of quantum fluctuations. Unusual patterns in this data lead us to employ three types of analyses: continuous wave detection, quasiperiodic signal identification through Fourier analysis, and machine learning-driven searches. These methods reveal quasiperiodic signals in multiple frequency ranges across the observed bandwidth and in multiple time periods within the observed duration, with some signals observed repeatedly over several years. Notably, a persistent and strong signal with a period of 1.38441248 +/- 10^-7 hours was found in the frequency range 8.6974 +/- 10^-3 GHz. To confirm our findings, we propose a statistical approach that takes into account the occurrence of coincidental patterns in the search process, and conclude that our detected signals exhibit a significance of 4-6 sigma. Furthermore, we speculate that free-karma emissions might be related to repeated explosive events on the stellar surface of certain variable stars, such as delta Scuti stars. If so, our discoveries represent the first recorded instances of quasiperiodic variability in these stars as detected through radio observations. If our findings hold up to future observation, we propose that the Arecibo 300-meter radio telescope, with its sensitive and narrowband receiver, would be well-suited to regularly monitoring these signals and potentially detecting similar variability in other star types. Additionally, we make the raw data and analysis code publicly available via an accompanying website.

To verify the significance of this finding, the authors propose a statistical approach that considers the occurrence of coincidental patterns in the search process and conclude that their detected signal exhibits a significance of 4-6 sigma. If this result holds up to future observation, it could represent the first recorded instance of quasiperiodic variability in free-karma emissions and potentially other variable stars as detected through radio observations.

increasing interest in using artificial
  neural networks to analyze energy spectra obtained from nuclear decay events.
  Traditional methods rely heavily on established patterns and rules-based
  interpretations; in contrast, neural networks can potentially uncover rare or
  disputed phenomena by automatically identifying patterns in energy spectra.
  However, to fully exploit the capabilities of such networks, it is essential to
  address issues related to systematic errors and fake signals created by background
  events and experimental limitations. To tackle these challenges, we propose
  new approaches to background subtraction, network training, and the evaluation
  of rare phenomenon searches using artificial neural networks.  We demonstrate
  these methods on a hypothetical case of searching for a rare decay pattern
  within a typical experimental setup, such as found in the BEPCII/BESIII experiment.  We show that by utilizing artificial neural networks to analyze energy spectra, researchers can optimize search regions, significantly narrowing them down from thousands to just a handful of candidates, thus greatly reducing the workload for human experts and significantly improving the effectiveness of rare phenomenon searches.  We also identify potential sources of systematic errors and provide a preliminary estimate of their impact on artificial neural network-based searches.  Finally, we highlight the potential applications of these methods to searches for other rare phenomena and in other fields of research.  We emphasize the importance of open-source code and publicly available artificial neural network models to ensure reproducibility and facilitate collaboration among researchers.  We stress the necessity of rigorous background analysis and cross-checks of results with different artificial neural network training datasets to prevent the discovery of fake signals.  We propose that future research directions could involve integrating expertise-based knowledge into artificial neural networks through the use of advisory systems, utilizing artificial neural networks to analyze multi-dimensional data sets, and exploring alternative network architectures that can provide insights into the underlying physics.  We also highlight the potential of BEPCII/BESIII to discover landmarks in energy spectra with the aid of artificial neural networks and identify areas in physics research that could be revolutionized by this approach.  We conclude that artificial neural network-based searches for rare phenomena are feasible and can be significantly improved by addressing issues related to systematic errors and fake signals.  We emphasize the crucial role of experimental design in providing clean and minimal fake signals, the importance of regular re-training of networks to account for changes in luminosity, and the potential of BEPCII/BESIII to discover landmarks in energy spectra with the aid of artificial neural networks. in solar flares investigates the formation of the solar spectrum through analyzing the spatial and temporal properties of emission lines in a specific wavelength range. A feature of this approach is the direct visualization of the flaring plasma's temperature and chemical composition. Prior observations with this setup detected the emergence of new emission lines in some solar flares, including one with a particularly strong line at 656.3 nanometers, not previously associated with known atomic or ionic transitions. Further investigation using a different spectrographic device revealed that this line was, in fact, a doublet consisting of two closely spaced lines at 656.3 and 658.3 nanometers. The source of this new emission is currently unknown but could originate from highly charged ions of certain elements such as silicon, magnesium, or nitrogen. The occurrence of these lines in solar flares holds significant implications for understanding the high-temperature plasma present in these events. The new line at 656.3 nanometers was observed in a strong X-class flare with significant energy release and in a weak C-class flare with less energy released, suggesting a possible association with particle acceleration taking place in the corona. The non-thermal nature of these lines is also evident in their exponential decline exceeding that of established lines, a phenomenon that can be explained by a non-thermal process known as the "non-thermal Maxwellian" distribution. The detection of these new lines in a solar flare with a prominent coronal source, the loop system of the M4.2 flare, provides additional evidence for the role of the "chorus" - a type of particle acceleration occurring in the corona - in producing the spectra observed in the flaring plasma. However, if neutrinos are indeed substantial, then even the tiniest axions would lose their weight-saving benefits.  Nevertheless, in a cosmologically significant period, particularly during the era of neutrino-Axon interaction, these minuscule axions could potentially make a difference.  In this work, we examine the impact of neutrino-Axon interaction on ULAs within a type I seesaw framework, focusing on the range where neutrinos aren't too light.  We determine the minimum mass of these tiny axions, which is crucial for neutrino-Axon interaction, and calculate how it influences ULAs across various neutrino flavors and mass ranges.  Moreover, we assess the effects on ULAs in the context of hot dark matter scenarios and as sub-dominant dark matter components.  We also explore the possibility of detecting these tiny axions through their interaction with active neutrinos in the universe.  We identify the relevant parameter ranges for these processes and discuss the potential of ongoing and future experiments in capturing evidence of these tiny axions.  We propose a new laboratory-based approach that utilizes a neutrino source to detect these minuscule axions, which could provide tangible evidence for these tiny particles.  We examine the sensitivity of this method to various neutrino-Axon interaction processes and the associated parameters, including the neutrino-Axon coupling constant, the mass of the active neutrinos, the mass of the ULA, and the density of the neutrino population.  We outline a feasible experiment design that aims to detect these tiny axions through their interaction with active neutrinos in the era of intense neutrino beams.  We discuss the potential of this method to detect these tiny axions in the context of existing and future intense neutrino beam facilities.  We estimate the required beam intensity and the associated experimental challenges to detect these tiny axions.  We also examine the potential of this method to detect these tiny axions through the emission of neutrino-Axon coannihilation products, such as electrons and positrons, in the context of a dedicated experiment inspired by the MACE/NEMO type.  We discuss the threshold energy of these products and the associated experimental reach to detect these tiny axions in the ultralight range.  We estimate the experimental reach to detect these tiny axions in the context of a dedicated experiment inspired by the MACE/NEMO type at the China Advanced Research Accelerator Facility (CARR).

However, existing efficient DHT implementations primarily focus on single-core processing and neglect parallelization capabilities. Chord is a particularly popular DHT that has been overlooked in this aspect, necessitating the development of our mpichord project. a previously undiscovered, broadly 
  extended gas cloud, designated Gaya, located within the direction of the 
  Scutum-Centaurus X-ray binary system. A prior survey failed to detect this 
  emission, likely due to its weak signal below the detection limit of the 
  earlier observation. Structural analysis of the cloud reveals an asymmetrical 
  shape with extensions on the northwest and southeast sides. The observed 
  velocity range of the cloud, inferred from HI spectra, spans from -23 to 
  16km/s and suggests that Gaya is moving towards the Sun. The cloud's total 
  mass is estimated at approximately 1.4 x 10^3 solar masses. Given its 
  distance from the Sun, the cloud is positioned between the Local Bulge and 
  the Scutum-Centaurus Arm, a dense molecular cloud system that includes the 
  well-known molecular cloud, W3.  The observed velocity of Gaya indicates 
  possible interaction between the cloud and the dense molecular arm, which 
  could be responsible for the star formation observed within W3.  Further 
  analysis of the radio spectrum of Gaya reveals a weak, continuous radio 
  emission pattern, indicating that the cloud contains both thermal and 
  non-thermal components of gas.  The discovery of Gaya expands our knowledge 
  of extended gas clouds within the Galaxy and suggests that a variety of 
  gas clouds, with different properties, are contributing to the formation 
  of stars, particularly within the Scutum-Centaurus Arm.  The detection 
  of a similar weak emission signal within the Cygnus X-1 direction, for 
  which we propose the name XShanti, also is reported.  The observed 
  structure of XShanti is extensionless, but it is notable for its 
  significantly higher non-thermal component of gas compared to Gaya, 
  and it is proposed that the masses of XShanti are too low for it to 
  influence nearby star formation.  The research presented here provides 
  the raw data associated with the research findings presented in the 
  paper "A Newly Discovered Extended Gas Cloud Associated with the 
  Scutum-Centaurus Arm" that was published in The Astrophysical Journal. 
  The data comprises HI spectra observed with the MeerKAT radio telescope.

Nonetheless, existing methods that utilize data consistency terms primarily focus on aligning measured images with actual data through division or normalization, rather than directly matching the brightness of images and actual data.  This issue is particularly apparent in MRI reconstruction tasks.  To address this limitation, we introduce a novel data consistency term that ensures the brightness of reconstructed images matches the brightness of actual data through a comparison based on exponential functions.  This comparison is necessary because MRI image intensity is influenced by nonlinear relationships.  We tested the proposed method with three different image reconstruction tasks, including Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and found that it outperforms traditional consistency terms in terms of accuracy as measured by a metric called Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR).  Specifically, with appropriate hyperparameter selection, the method yielded reconstruction results that were 3.03, 2.45, and 1.95 times more accurate than the comparative methods for image acquisition protocols known as Cardiac Cine MRI at the scales of whole heart, liver, and liver with insertion of a coil, respectively.  Furthermore, the proposed method was robust to the selection of hyperparameters and exhibited robust performance across different scales.  To facilitate widespread adoption, we made the proposed method's code publicly available.   for the Comparative Method is made available. 

  A particular challenge in deep learning that this paper addresses is the instability 
  of estimates derived from importance sampling. A key factor contributing to this 
  instability is the variance of the estimates, which is not adequately accounted for 
  in current techniques. A novel method, called the Comparative Method, is introduced 
  that reduces variance and results in a more stable performance. This method involves 
  a specialized comparison that helps control the variance and was found to outperform 
  a range of baseline methods in a variety of scenarios. 

  A particular scenario that this paper examines is the situation in which a function 
  f is difficult to compute directly, but it is easy to obtain related functions 
  g and h, which are linear combinations of f. In this case, a Comparative Method can 
  be applied to estimate f by comparing g and h, and this approach is shown to 
  minimize the variance of the estimates. 

  A general framework for the Comparative Method is also presented along with an 
  explanation for its connection to the reverse hypercube method. A key advantage of 
  the Comparative Method is that it can be applied to a wide range of scenarios, 
  which include the estimation of high-dimensional integrals and the sampling of 
  complex probability distributions. 

  A particular application of the Comparative Method is shown to be a sophisticated 
  version of the VAE Monte Carlo method that was previously introduced. This method 
  involves combining the Comparative Method with the reweighing technique from

The study is of a search for direct production of top and light neutralinos in the $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, 33 fb$^{-1}$ dataset obtained from the LHC.  The analysis focuses on events featuring a single high-energy jet identified as originating from a top or bottom quark, accompanied by two light neutralinos that decay into soft leptons and soft hadronic activity.  The detection of these events is complicated by the presence of soft multiplicity and imperfect jet identification.  The analysis employs advanced techniques such as multivariate event identification and large-scale smearings to mimic the soft multiplicity, allowing for the rejection of combinatorial background sources.  The search extends the exclusion region in the stop-neutralino mass plane, incorporating the $s$-channel production scenario that was previously unmapped.  The searched-for events exhibit characteristics similar to those of typical top quark production events, highlighting the importance of further advances in jet identification techniques for future searches.  The analysis of the searched dataset rules out the existence of light stops below 750 GeV for a range of neutralino masses, and the search for a light bottom quark partner remains an open question.   uncertainty in type Ia supernovae light curves can be significantly

This problem is equivalent to solving the generalization of the well-known "congruence partitioning problem" with additional constraints. In fungi, specific genes are linked to particular ecological and biological functions, but the relationship between genomic localization and gene activity remains largely unexplored. This study investigates spatial correlations between genomic features and gene expression patterns across multiple tissues in the fungus Aspergillus niger. By applying spatial transcriptomics and an exhaustive mapping of chromatin structure and protein occupancy, we identified numerous genomic features associated with quiet or active gene expression, as well as various transcription factor binding sites. Notably, a significant pattern emerged where genetic features associated with gene activity display a gradient that reflects the physical distance between genes and their nearest chromosomal replication origin. This finding is particularly intriguing as previous research in yeast suggested a gradient inversely related to replication origin distance. By integrating data from multiple sources and analyzing chromatin structure, we found that a change in nucleosome occupancy patterns plays a crucial role in determining local gene expression patterns. Conversely, factors influencing global gene expression, such as RNA polymerase binding, do not follow the origin-to-telomere gradient. This research provides a comprehensive framework for predicting gene expression from a dataset of Aspergillus niger chromatin structure and highlights the significance of local nucleosome occupancy patterns in mediating replication origin effects on gene activity. requires automated systems to naturally interact with each other, a process that enables them to exchange information securely through peer-to-peer connections.
  For such systems to function effectively, their automated components must be able to establish reliable connections with each other, a process known as transport protocol establishment.
  Currently, automated online communication systems exchange information securely through encrypted connections, making it difficult for humans to analyze system behavior.
  As a result, developers often lack insight into the automated processes that underlie these systems and must rely on incomplete documentation.
  To address this limitation, we developed an automated testing framework that allows human observers to see the underlying protocol exchange when a system is connected to another system automatically.
  To achieve this, the framework generates test code that mimics human analysis of protocol exchange exchange based on human observation of a specific example, which is then automated.
  The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through an investigation of three complex automated online communication systems, showing that it identifies the underlying transport protocol established by the systems' automated components. 
  The development of the framework also sheds light on the underlying protocols of three widely used technologies: WebSockets, SPDY, and HTTP/2.
  The testing code for these examples is included with the distribution of the paper as a reference for other developers working with similar systems.

We contend that regularized neural networks, with their ability to handle excessive parameters, can lead to improved generalized performance due to internal regularization that prevents the network from capturing trivial patterns. From this perspective, we show that the ability of neural networks to resist trivial pattern learning can be measured and charaterized as a form of statistical learning theory incompatibility, which varies as a function of the network's capacity and requires compliance with one of three incompatible relationships that network designers, researchers, and practitioners must be aware of in order to ensure generalized performance. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the inherent resistance to trivial pattern learning of dense neural networks is susceptible to overfitting when working with sparse regularization, leading to the inferior performance of sparse methods and highlighting the potential risks of employing sparse regularization for feature selection. We support these claims with a series of experiments covering both linear and nonlinear machine learning models, as well as real-world applications in classification and regression tasks. We contend that considering the statistical learning theory implications of dense neural networks can lead to a deeper comprehension of deep learning and suggested exploring alternative methods to dense regularization-based feature selection. Through applications of the quantum maximum entropy method, we demonstrate the non-equivalence of quantum states associated with distinct unitary processes. Furthermore, we explore the case of multiple system non-equivalence, expressing the non-classicality of bosonic quantum computations using two-mode squeezed vacuum states. A concise summary of our findings along with potential avenues for research emerges from our study.
